summary: For ages 10–11: use negative numbers in directed real-world contexts (temperature, bank balance, sea level) and calculate intervals across zero as a distance on the number line. The key insight is that an across-zero interval decomposes at zero into two magnitudes that ADD (e.g. −2 to 3 = 2 + 3 = 5), and that ordering depends on direction, not digit size (−5 sits below −3 even though 5 > 3). Signed +/−/× arithmetic rules are deferred to later study.
misconceptions: Treating −5 as larger than −3 because '5 > 3' (ignoring direction)
Counting the interval across zero without including the step onto/over 0, or double-counting zero
Adding the numbers instead of finding a distance (−5 to 3 answered as −2)
Believing there is no number between −1 and 1 other than described, or that zero is negative/positive
Reading a fall in temperature as a rise because the digit gets 'bigger' (−2 to −8 seen as warming)

activities.title: Dragging across zero on a vertical number line (thermometer)
steps: Set a start value (e.g. −2°C) and an end value (e.g. 3°C) on a vertical number line scaled like a thermometer.
Drag a marker from the start up through zero to the end, watching the interval light up as two arcs meeting at zero: '2 below → 0' and '0 → 3'.
Read the running interval as it decomposes: 2 + 3 = 5, rather than a single subtraction.
Switch the context (temperature → sea-level cross-section → bank balance, e.g. −£120 below zero and £350 above) while the same number line stays, and repeat the drag.
Compare the positions of −5 and −3 on the scale and state which is lower and why.
activities.insight: An interval that spans zero is the sum of the two distances on each side of zero; direction (not the size of the digit) sets the order of negative numbers, so −5 lies below −3.

activities.title: Explain-the-error dialogue: 'convince me on the line'
steps: Consider a claim such as: 'The temperature fell from 3°C to −5°C, so it dropped 2 degrees.'
Decide whether it is right or wrong, and use a number line to justify your answer.
State where zero is in the journey and how far you travel on each side of it.
Explain in words why the answer is not simply 5 − 3 = 2.
activities.insight: Verbalising why the zero crossing must be counted exposes the 'subtract the magnitudes' error and reinforces that the interval is the sum of both sides.

activities.title: Ordering and interval consolidation
steps: Order a set such as −7, −3, 0, 2, 5 from lowest to highest and place them on a number line.
Find the interval from −7 to 5 by splitting at zero: 7 (below) + 5 (above) = 12.
Set a temperature after a stated fall (e.g. start 3°C, fall 8 degrees → −5°C) by marking it on the line.
Find the difference between a balance of −£120 and £350 and check it against the 'add both sides' method: 120 + 350 = 470.
activities.insight: Ordering negatives and computing across-zero intervals become reliable once the number-line intuition is applied consistently across contexts.

checkQuestion: Set the problems and watch the working: 'The temperature falls from 3°C to −5°C — what is the drop? A bank balance goes from −£120 to £350 — what is the difference? What is the interval from −7 to 5?' Watch how they handle the zero crossing.
checkAnswer: 8 degrees; £470; 12 — found by adding the distance on each side of zero (or counting across it).
